Excerpted from media reports:

Federal authorities raided three San Francisco medical marijuana clubs Wednesday, and investigators arrested at least 13 people as part of an alleged organized crime operation using the clubs as a front to launder money.

The raids were the first in the Bay Area since the U.S. Supreme Court ruled two weeks ago that the federal government had the authority to prosecute patients despite state law.

Twenty people were charged in an indictment that federal authorities planned to unseal today. San Francisco sheriff's officials said Wednesday night that 11 men and two women were in the county jail in connection with the case and would appear in federal court today.

Authorities said the raids were the culmination of a lengthy investigation of an operation whose members were mostly of Asian descent and living in San Francisco and Oakland. They said that the operation controlled at least 10 warehouses where marijuana was grown in large quantities.

"It's not the pot clubs per se'' that were targets, said one law enforcement official, who asked not to be named because the indictments were still under seal. "It's not an attack on medical marijuana. This is an organized crime group that is using the whole pot club thing as a front.''

San Francisco Mayor Gavin Newsom declined to comment on the federal raids but nodded affirmatively when asked whether he believed they reached beyond the issue of medical marijuana.

This is not entirely new. San Francisco police have raided a dozen large indoor marijuana-growing operations, mostly in flats in the Sunset District, in the last two years. Investigators say at least some of these illegal home operations were connected to the new case.  

Others were not and should not have been raided.

SF Police Chief Heather Fong said her narcotics officers had taken part in Wednesday's roundup of suspects but had not raided the dispensaries. Local medical marijuana backers criticized the SF police participation, but they may have been something of a restraining force in this context. Who watches the watchman?

City policy recognizes cannabis clubs under Proposition 215. As a result, "we don't enter pot clubs'' to make marijuana arrests, Fong said.

At one point this spring, San Francisco was home to 44 medical marijuana dispensaries, more than any other city in the nation. Matt Dorsey of the city attorney's office said San Francisco now had 35 storefront dispensaries. Those don't include clubs that operate by appointment only or delivery-only service.

Supervisor Ross Mirkarimi, who has spent months working on new rules, said the city had to find a way to separate legitimate operations from illegitimate ones.

"The absence of laws only puts out a welcome mat for potential problems, '' he said. "That's how we got to the place where we are today.''

Supervisor Gerardo Sandoval, whose district includes two of the clubs, has also called for improved city monitoring but said he hoped Wednesday's raids were "not a pretext to meddle in San Francisco's well- established medical marijuana policies."

"It's pretty clear the Bush administration is not very happy about San Francisco's efforts," Sandoval said. "If there's money laundering or organized crime involved, then by all means we welcome federal law enforcement. But I have to ask myself, 'Why now?' "

One sad note: for some reason the feds chose the same day to finally drop the other jackboot and indict Dr. Marion Fry and her husband Dale C.  Schafer. They were arrested at their home and pleaded not guilty in federal court in Sacramento to charges of distributing and manufacturing at least 100 marijuana plants. The actual raid took place in 2002.

But Saskatchewan patients who want to try the new whole cannabis derivative may have to hunt around to find a doctor willing to prescribe it.  And at $124.95 for a 10-day supply, users will also be reaching deep into their own pockets -- the Sativex isn't covered by any public or private health-care plans.

It will $124.95 (plus service charges, which makes it $150 per vial) for a vial containing 50 sprays, with the average daily dose being 5 sprays. (The Canadian dollar is around 80 cents US.

In other words, it will cost users $3 a spray, or $12-15 a day for the average user.  I hope that this will prove helpful to the many Canadians that currently suffer from MS neuropathic pain who might not have access to a safe supply of cannabis, but with this "black-market" level price, Sativex may be too cost prohibitive for many of those who might benefit from it.

Jan Britz, a registered nurse and clinic co-ordinator of the Saskatoon MS Clinic at City Hospital, said clinic staff will carefully examine the drug and its potential side-effects before doctors prescribe it to any patients.

"Because we're not a big promoter of the use of marijuana in itself, what we have requested is being able to see copies of the clinical trials that were done, just so we have more information about the medication before we would ever consider prescribing it," Britz said.

"The last thing you want to do is bring harm to the patients in your prescribing practice," she said.
See

Canadian MS patient and genuine human rights hero, Grant Krieger has been battling the MS establishment and other quacks for at least a decade.
See

and links

Canada was the first country in the world to approve Sativex for use in MS patients who experience neuropathic pain, a sensation Britz described as an intense burning discomfort deep inside that sometimes tingles like pins and needles.

Sativex is an extract from whole cannabis containing active ingredients delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol ( THC ) and cannabidiol ( CBD ) and all the other cannabinoids and other ingredients about which relatively little is known.

Patients squirt the peppermint-flavoured spray under their tongue or in the side of their cheek four or five times a day to dull the pain.

Allan Gordon, a neurologist and director of the Wasser Pain Management Centre at Mount Sinai Hospital in Toronto, said, "It's quite exciting. My patients are very anxious to try it."

Laurie Murphy, acting director of client services with the Multiple Sclerosis Society of Canada's Saskatchewan chapter, said she's glad patients will have a legal alternative to smoking marijuana.

Gordon said a third of the patients his clinic has seen have tried self-medicating with marijuana at least once.
See
 There Are Already Almost 600,000 Canadian Medical Marijuana Users, But Health Canada Has Only Approved 40  2 Articles With Interesting Lesson In Spin.

"I think it's wonderful ...  there's possibly a treatment out there that has less side-effects, that might be able to still treat this neuropathic pain that is very difficult to treat," Murphy said.  "I'm very happy that they have another option that's available to them that's legal so they don't feel that they have to sneak around to get something that might give them some relief."

Despite the risks of black market cannabis , Murphy isn't sure dedicated marijuana users will relinquish their pipes in exchange for this new alternative.

"I don't know that somebody who was already receiving benefit from a marijuana joint is going to be willing to give that up that easily," she said.  

Britz said she's also concerned the drug could be abused by users who consume it to try and get high.

"Once the patient has filled that prescription, you don't have a lot of control over how they're using it," she said.

She hopes the cost of the drug will deter users from taking more than they need.

Currently, the drug is only approved for use by Canadian MS patients.  Gordon said studies are ongoing to see if the painkiller will work for other types of nerve pain, such as in diabetes.

Excerpted from The Independent (London):

GWs Losses were pared to UKP 5.1m in the first six months of the year, but the company is still burning through more than UKP 1m a month and knows that regulators are demanding bigger and more statistically significant trials if Sativex is to get on the market in Europe.  Although there will be some money coming in from Canadian sales, the company's UKP 16.2m cash pile will be whittled away by the end of next year.

Encumbered with a history of over-optimism, the company knows it will not be able to raise cash from shareholders at the current price.  So it is hoping instead to sell marketing rights to Sativex in continental Europe as it has done in the UK and Canada.  Unless Canadian sales turn out to be spectacular ( unlikely in a country which already allows MS sufferers to smoke cannabis ), these deals might not bring in enough.  Avoid.

The Vancouver Island Compassion Society (VICS) is pleased to announce that on Wednesday June 8th VICS founder/director Philippe Lucas and Dr. Shannon Hamersley received "unconditional approval" by an independent  Institutional  review board to conduct a smoked-cannabis and chronic pain study at it the  society's headquarters in Victoria, B.C.

The study, titled "A comparison of the effects of smoked whole-plant cannabis of different THC concentrations in non-treatment naive patients with chronic  pain" will be the first high-THC, smoked cannabis and chronic pain double-blind clinical protocol in North America, and the first clinical trial to ever be conducted in cooperation with a non-profit medicinal cannabis compassion society.

The dose-response protocol will compare the analgesic effects of cannabis preparations of three different strengths (0%THC placebo, 10-12%THC, and 16-18%THC) for analgesia and other effects (including appetite, energy, and sleep) on 15 chronic pain sufferers who have not responded to conventional pharmaceutical treatments.

Lucas said,  "Our next step is to submit the protocol to Health Canada for final approval, and then we'll be on our way towards further understanding the therapeutic potential of this incredible herb."

Excerpted from wire reports

The leftist Zapatista movement closed its offices and sent rebel leaders into hiding as a ''precautionary defensive measure'' while members discuss the future of their fight against Mexico's government, the group's military commander said Tuesday.

In one statement, Subcomandante Marcos said the actions allowed the rebels to discuss their next move.

In a second, he boasted that the Zapatistas have completed a military reorganization begun in 2002 and they have the capacity to survive as an organization, an attack or enemy action that tries to stop our leadership or totally annihilate us.

Marcos said the alert was necessary because when the group called a series of strategy meetings in 1995, then President Ernesto Zedillo ordered a military offensive seeking the rebel commander's arrest.

Despite Marcos' two communiques, it was unclear what motivated the Zapatistas' strategy sessions.

One factor could be the country's presidential elections, scheduled for July 2006. A more immediate reason might be that the Mexican army announced Monday it had raided nearly 10 acres of marijuana plantations in the rebels' ''area of influence'' in the southern state of Chiapas. The rebels, who rattled Mexico with a brief armed uprising in January 1994, oppose any military presence in their communities and deny there are any drugs or contraband.

The Zapatista movement, which champions Indian rights, operated in secrecy for about a decade before its rebellion. Within a month of fighting, the rebels entered an uneasy cease-fire with the government that was broken only by the brief government offensive in 1995.

Ruben Aguilar, a spokesman for President Vicente Fox, said Tuesday there was no provocation for the alert and added the government was willing to talk with the rebels.

In Oventic, a Zapatista political and cultural center 460 miles southeast of Mexico City, a hastily drawn sign on a locked door declared: ''Closed for red alert.''
